name: Feng-Aroma Baijiu
description: The phoenix aroma from Shaanxi, sitting between the light and strong styles. Fermented in earthen pits that are rebuilt annually rather than aged for centuries, then rested in wicker baskets sealed with wax.
funFact: Xifeng's storage vessels are woven baskets lined with pig's blood and beeswax, a method that imparts a specific flavour no other baijiu has.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, with food, and with toasts. It is a good bridge for anyone who finds strong-aroma too pungent and light-aroma too plain.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented in annually rebuilt earth pits, then basket-aged.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum with barley and pea qu

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Wax-sealed wicker baskets rather than earthenware jars

composition.process: Rebuilding the pits each year is the opposite of the strong-aroma approach and deliberately so.

name: Sesame-Aroma Baijiu
description: The chi aroma from Shandong, created in the 1950s and the newest of the recognised baijiu categories. Smells distinctly of toasted sesame, which is unusual enough that it earned its own classification.
funFact: It was identified as a distinct aroma category only in 1957, making it the youngest of the major baijiu styles by several centuries.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with food. The sesame note is genuinely reminiscent of the oil, and it pairs remarkably well with northern Chinese dishes that already use it.

composition.summary: Sorghum, wheat and bran fermented in brick-lined pits.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum with wheat, bran and barley qu

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Solid-state, in brick and mud pits

composition.process: The sesame note comes from the fermentation, not from any sesame — none is used.

name: Mixed-Aroma Baijiu
description: The jian aroma, deliberately combining techniques from the sauce, strong and light styles in one spirit. A twentieth-century innovation that treats the classical categories as a palette rather than a set of rules.
funFact: Baijiu aroma categories are formally defined by Chinese national standards, and adding a new one requires state recognition.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups with a meal. It is the most approachable style for a newcomer, because no single characteristic dominates the way sauce-aroma umami or strong-aroma funk does.

composition.summary: Techniques from several aroma families combined in one production process.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended methods drawn from sauce, strong and light aroma production

composition.process: Deliberate hybridisation rather than regional tradition, which makes it unusual in a conservative category.

name: Medicinal-Aroma Baijiu
description: The yao aroma from Guizhou, fermented with over a hundred medicinal herbs worked into the qu starter. Herbal, bitter-edged and closer to a tonic than the other baijiu styles.
funFact: Dongjiu's qu starter incorporates more than a hundred Chinese medicinal herbs, which is why the category is named for medicine rather than for a flavour.

serve.how: Room temperature, small cups, with food. The herbal bitterness makes it the baijiu most likely to appeal to an amaro drinker, and the least likely to appeal to a whisky one.

composition.summary: Sorghum fermented with a herb-laden qu in stone pits.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sorghum, rice, and qu containing 100+ herbs

composition.process: The herbs go into the starter culture rather than being infused afterwards, so they drive fermentation as well as flavour.

name: Soba Shochu
description: Buckwheat shochu, first made in Miyazaki in 1973 and now a category of its own. Lighter and more delicate than barley or sweet potato, with the faint nuttiness of soba noodles.
funFact: Buckwheat is not a grain but a seed related to rhubarb, which is why soba shochu is naturally gluten-free.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with cold water
serve.how: On the rocks or mizuwari with cold water. It is among the gentlest shochu styles, which makes it a good introduction, and it is exceptional alongside actual soba noodles.

composition.summary: Buckwheat fermented with koji and single-distilled.
composition.process: Vacuum distillation at low pressure preserves the delicate nutty character heat would strip.

name: Kasutori Shochu
description: Distilled from sake lees — the pressed rice solids left after sake is made — rather than from fresh grain. A genuine circular product, and unmistakably sake-scented.
funFact: Sake lees, kasu, are also used to pickle vegetables and marinate fish, so distilling them is one of several traditional uses for what is technically a by-product.

serve.how: Cool and neat, or on the rocks. It smells strikingly of sake, which surprises people expecting a neutral spirit, and it is superb with the same food sake suits.

composition.summary: Sake lees fermented further and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Sake kasu — pressed lees from sake production

composition.process: Lees still carry rice starch and yeast, so they ferment again readily before distilling.

name: Goma Shochu
description: Sesame shochu, a rare Japanese style in which roasted sesame seeds are fermented alongside rice. Deeply nutty and aromatic, and produced by only a handful of distillers.
funFact: Sesame is expensive and low-yielding as a fermentable, which is why the style has never grown beyond a few producers.

serve.temp: on the rocks or with hot water
serve.how: On the rocks, or oyuwari with hot water, which lifts the sesame aroma dramatically. It is one of the few shochu styles that genuinely improves with heat.

composition.summary: Roasted sesame seeds fermented with rice and koji, then distilled.
composition.process: Roasting the seeds before fermentation is what develops the aroma the style is built on.

name: Awamori Kusu
description: Awamori aged at least three years in earthenware, traditionally by topping older jars from younger ones. Some family kusu is said to have been maintained for over a century before the war destroyed most of it.
funFact: Almost all of Okinawa's pre-war kusu was destroyed in the Battle of Okinawa in 1945, so genuinely ancient stock effectively no longer exists.

serve.temp: room temp or on the rocks
serve.how: Neat at room temperature in a small cup, or on the rocks. Okinawans traditionally cut it with water and let it sit overnight before serving, which softens it noticeably.

composition.summary: Awamori aged three years or more in clay pots by fractional topping.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Long-grain Thai rice with black koji

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum three years in earthenware; traditional systems run far longer

composition.process: Clay is slightly porous, so the spirit oxidises slowly in a way glass or steel would not allow.

name: Sato
description: Thai glutinous rice spirit from the northeast, made with a traditional starter cake and distilled at village scale. The rural counterpart to commercial lao khao, and central to Isan hospitality.
funFact: Home production was illegal in Thailand for most of the twentieth century and was only partially liberalised in the 2000s, driving a revival of village distilling.

serve.how: Neat in small measures, shared, with food. In Isan it appears at every festival and family gathering, and refusing the first glass is difficult to do gracefully.

composition.summary: Glutinous rice fermented with a look pang starter and pot-distilled.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Look pang — a yeast and mould starter cake

composition.process: The same fermented base drunk unfiltered and undistilled is also called sato, which causes confusion.

name: Rượu Nếp
description: Northern Vietnamese sticky rice spirit, distilled from the fermented glutinous rice that is also eaten as a dish in its own right. Sweeter and rounder than the southern rượu đế.
funFact: The fermented rice itself is eaten at the Tết Đoan Ngọ festival, traditionally on an empty stomach and first thing in the morning.

serve.how: Room temperature in small cups, poured for others and drunk together. Northern Vietnamese households make it for Tết and it appears at weddings and ancestor ceremonies year-round.

composition.summary: Glutinous rice fermented with a herb-laden starter and pot-distilled.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Men rượu starter, often containing herbs

composition.process: Sticky rice ferments sweeter than ordinary rice, which carries into the distillate.

name: Aguardiente Antioqueño
description: Colombia's national spirit: anise-flavoured cane alcohol, produced under state monopoly with each department bottling its own brand. Fiercely regional — Antioqueños and Caleños will argue about it at length.
funFact: Colombian departments hold the production monopoly, so each has its own aguardiente brand and defending yours is a matter of regional identity.

serve.how: Cold, neat, in small glasses, shared from the bottle over a long evening. Colombians drink it with food and music rather than as a shot, and the sin azúcar versions are drier and increasingly preferred.

composition.summary: Sugarcane spirit flavoured with anise and sweetened.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Aniseed, plus sugar in the standard versions

composition.process: Departmental monopolies date to the colonial era and still fund regional budgets.

name: Absinthe Verte
description: The green style, coloured naturally by steeping herbs in the finished spirit so chlorophyll bleeds in. That colour fades to amber with age, which is how a genuine old bottle is recognised.
funFact: Naturally coloured absinthe turns amber over years as the chlorophyll degrades — a bottle described as feuille morte, dead leaf, is old rather than spoiled.

serve.glass: Absinthe glass with a slotted spoon
serve.how: Three to five parts iced water dripped slowly over a sugar cube on a slotted spoon. The louche should build gradually. No flames — burning the sugar is a 1990s invention that scorches the herbs.

composition.summary: Wormwood, anise and fennel distilled, then steeped with herbs for colour.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Grande wormwood, green anise, fennel; petite wormwood and hyssop for colouring

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled, then a second cold steep for natural colour

composition.process: Artificially coloured absinthe stays green forever, which is the giveaway.

name: Absinthe Blanche
description: The clear style, bottled straight off the still with no colouring step. Swiss in origin, where clandestine producers kept it colourless through the ban so it could pass as something innocent.
funFact: Swiss bootleggers kept it clear precisely because a colourless bottle was easier to explain to the authorities than a vivid green one — the style outlived the reason for it.

serve.how: Iced water dripped slowly, three to five parts to one. Blanche louches to a bright opalescent white rather than a cloudy green, and it tends to be cleaner and more herbal than verte.

composition.summary: Wormwood and anise distilled and bottled without a colouring steep.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled once with botanicals; no second steep

composition.process: Skipping the colouring step also skips the extra herb tannin, which is why blanche often tastes brighter.

name: Dill Aquavit
description: The Danish and Swedish variation in which dill leads rather than caraway. Fresher and greener than the classic style, and built for the summer table rather than the winter one.
funFact: Scandinavian aquavit must legally take its dominant flavour from caraway or dill — those two, and no others, define the category in EU law.

serve.how: From the freezer, in small measures, with food rather than before it. Dill aquavit belongs with crayfish and new potatoes in a way the caraway styles do not — it is a summer spirit.

composition.summary: Grain or potato spirit redistilled with dill as the lead botanical.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Dill leading, with fennel, coriander and citrus peel

composition.process: Dill's aromatics are fragile, so it goes in later and gentler than caraway would.

name: Taffel Akvavit
description: The classic Danish table aquavit, clear and caraway-forward, unaged and bottled at 45%. What Danes mean when they say akvavit without qualifying it further.
funFact: Taffel means table, and the name marks it as the everyday version rather than an aged or special bottling.

serve.how: Freezer cold, in small measures, with the meal. Danish tradition is a beer alongside and a toast before each glass, with eye contact — skipping the eye contact is the part visitors get wrong.

composition.summary: Grain spirit redistilled with caraway and citrus, unaged.
composition.process: Bottling unaged and clear is what distinguishes it from the oak-rested Norwegian styles.

name: Kruidenbitter
description: The Dutch herbal bitter category, of which Beerenburg is the most famous example. Juniper spirit steeped with gentian, bay and laurel, drunk cold and largely by people who grew up with it.
funFact: Amsterdam spice merchants sold the herb blends over the counter so drinkers could steep their own jenever at home, which is how the category began.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass. Dutch and Frisian drinkers take it before or after food rather than with it, and often alongside a beer.

composition.summary: Jenever or neutral spirit steeped with a fixed herb blend.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, bay, laurel, juniper berry, and a dozen more

composition.process: Maceration rather than distillation keeps the herbs green and raw rather than polished.

name: Horincă
description: The Maramureș variant of Romanian fruit brandy, double or triple distilled to a considerably higher strength than țuică. Made from plums or apples in the far north, and a matter of local pride.
funFact: Names shift by region across Romania — țuică in the south, horincă in Maramureș, pălincă in Transylvania, jinars in parts of the west — for broadly the same tradition.

serve.how: Room temperature, neat, in small glasses, offered on arrival. Northern Romanian households serve it warmed with honey and pepper in winter, which is called a fiartă.

composition.summary: Plums or apples fermented and distilled two or three times.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Plums, apples or pears from Maramureș orchards

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double or triple distillation in copper

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Sometimes rested in mulberry or oak

composition.process: The extra distillation is what separates it from țuică, and locals consider the strength a point of honour.

name: Medovina Rakija
description: Honey-fermented rakija from the Balkans — distinct from medovača, which is rakija sweetened with honey after the fact. Here the honey is fermented and distilled, which is a different drink entirely.
funFact: Fermenting honey is the basis of mead, the oldest known alcoholic drink, so distilling it produces something closer to a mead brandy than to a fruit rakija.

serve.how: Room temperature in a small pour after a meal. It is rounder and more floral than fruit rakija, and worth tasting beside a medovača to see the difference between fermenting honey and adding it.

composition.summary: Honey fermented into mead and then distilled.
composition.process: Honey ferments slowly and needs nutrient additions, which is why honey distillates are rare everywhere.
